title: Workflow Jobs and Their Properties knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Workflow Jobs and Their Properties?
options: A job has an identifier and runner, may declare `needs` dependencies and `if` conditions, and can set timeouts and failure behavior.
Give every job write permission to avoid troubleshooting authorization errors.
Print all environment variables and event payloads to make the run easier to debug.
Run untrusted pull-request code in the same job that holds production credentials.
questions.answer_key: A job has an identifier and runner, may declare `needs` dependencies and `if` conditions, and can set timeouts and failure behavior.
questions.explanation: This is the central behavior of workflow jobs and their properties: A job has an identifier and runner, may declare `needs` dependencies and `if` conditions, and can set timeouts and failure behavior. Validate configuration and behavior against the current official reference before production use.

questions.prompt: How should a reviewer verify a change related to workflow jobs and their properties?
options: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
Assume the workflow is correct as soon as the YAML file is committed.
Retry every failure without looking at the exit code or preserving evidence.
Publish the workflow to production before reviewing its triggers and permissions.
questions.answer_key: Run a controlled test or static check, inspect the relevant job and step result, and compare the evidence with the stated acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Reliable verification uses observable evidence. For this lesson, consider: A job has an identifier and runner, may declare `needs` dependencies and `if` conditions, and can set timeouts and failure behavior. A syntax check alone cannot prove remote execution, permissions, or deployment behavior.
